questions.question: Define the Industrial Revolution and describe its four connected changes, with one example of each.
questions.expected_answer: The Industrial Revolution was the change from an economy based on farming and handicraft to one based on machine manufacture in factories, powered by water and then steam, from about 1750 in Britain. Machinery: the spinning jenny, water frame, spinning mule and power loom in cotton. Power: water wheels and then Watt and Boulton's steam engines, which let factories be built in towns near coal. The factory system: workers, machines and power brought together under supervision, as at Arkwright's Cromford mill of 1771. Transport: canals such as the Bridgewater Canal of 1761 and railways such as the Liverpool and Manchester of 1830.

questions.question: Explain how the Industrial Revolution changed the population, settlement and social structure of Britain, using figures and dates.
questions.expected_answer: Population of England and Wales grew from about 6 million in 1750 to about 18 million in 1851 and over 32 million in 1901. People moved from the countryside to towns, called urbanisation; in 1851 more people in Britain lived in towns than in the countryside for the first time, and Manchester grew from about 25 000 around 1770 to over 300 000 by 1850. New classes formed: an industrial middle class of owners, bankers, engineers and professionals who gained the vote in 1832, and a large working class of wage earners who gained the vote in stages in 1867 and 1884.

questions.question: Describe how factory work changed time and family life, and summarise the debate about whether living standards rose during the Industrial Revolution.
questions.expected_answer: The factory bell and the machines set the hours and pace; days of 12 to 14 hours, six days a week, were common, with fines or dismissal for lateness or slowness. Work moved out of the home, so family members worked separately under different bosses, and women and children were a large share of early textile workers. Optimists point to rising real wages after about 1850 and cheap goods such as cotton clothes, soap, tea and sugar. Pessimists point to long hours, dangerous work, child labour, crowded unhealthy towns and evidence that health declined in the early decades. Many historians conclude that gains came mainly after 1850 and the first generations paid a heavy price.
